anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: A static mismatch between the physical data model (tables, indexes, partitions, constraints, data types) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing otherwise well-formed queries into broad scans or non-covering lookups.
Transaction Lock Contention Anomaly: Excessive or conflicting lock requests among concurrent transactions that lead to long blocking chains or deadlocks, degrading throughput and provoking rollbacks.

When these two root causes co-exist, the system exhibits a blend of I/O-heavy access paths and severe lock queuing. Queries that should have been quick, selective index probes instead scan whole tables or large index ranges, acquiring and holding many row, page, or even table locks for extended periods. This inflates lock footprints, lengthens critical-section times, and causes cascades of blockers and waiters. Observable symptoms include simultaneous spikes in logical/physical I/O, CPU usage, lock wait time, deadlock frequency, connection-pool exhaustion, and dramatic variance in response times; execution plans show scans while lock-diagnostic views reveal growing wait chains often ending in deadlock victim rollbacks.

Causally, poor schema and index design enlarges the scope and duration of locking: missing or non-covering indexes force full scans that touch many rows, causing transactions to acquire more locks and hold them longer. The broadened lock scope increases the probability of conflict with other concurrent transactions, intensifying lock contention. In turn, prolonged blocking and repeated deadlocks further delay statement completion, keeping scans active even longer and amplifying the performance penalty of the design flaw. The feedback loop between inefficient access paths and escalating lock waits can drive the database into a state of chronic congestion where both throughput and user experience deteriorate sharply.

entry.cause_analysis: The failure is typically associated with a general engine-level execution problem surfaced by the official error catalogue, but its precise trigger must be interpreted together with workload context and surrounding evidence.
entry.solution_guidance: Review the surrounding workload, official description, and engine state to determine whether the issue is rooted in SQL logic, resource pressure, configuration, or environmental instability.
